reference.source: Kelley & Firestein's Textbook of Rheumatology / EULAR systemic sclerosis guidance
clinicalPearls: Presents with abrupt severe (often malignant) hypertension and rapidly rising creatinine, usually in early diffuse systemic sclerosis
Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies and recent glucocorticoid exposure are important risk factors
A microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with thrombocytopenia frequently accompanies the renal injury
Prompt angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition is the cornerstone of treatment and can rescue kidney function even after dialysis is started
Headache, visual disturbance, encephalopathy, or acute pulmonary oedema may reflect the hypertensive emergency
A minority of cases are normotensive, which can delay recognition and worsen outcome
Glucocorticoids should be used cautiously and at the lowest effective exposure in at-risk patients because they may precipitate crisis
reference.pathophysiology: Scleroderma renal crisis arises from obliterative vasculopathy of the renal arcuate and interlobular arteries, with intimal proliferation and luminal narrowing reducing renal blood flow. Consequent activation of the renin-angiotensin system produces severe hypertension, which further injures the vessel walls in a self-amplifying cycle. Endothelial damage in the small vessels drives a thrombotic microangiopathy with mechanical fragmentation of red cells and platelet consumption. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition interrupts the renin-angiotensin drive and is therefore central to management.
additionalDifferentials: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura or haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis with renal involvement
additionalInvestigations: Serial blood pressure measurement and renal function monitoring
Blood film for schistocytes with haptoglobin, lactate dehydrogenase, and platelet count
Anti-RNA polymerase III and systemic sclerosis autoantibody profiling
ADAMTS13 activity to help exclude thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
Renal biopsy in selected diagnostically uncertain cases
redFlags: Accelerated or malignant hypertension with encephalopathy or seizures
Flash pulmonary oedema from hypertensive heart failure
Falling platelets with schistocytes signalling thrombotic microangiopathy
reference.prognosis: Before the era of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition renal crisis was almost uniformly fatal; timely blood pressure control now allows many patients to recover renal function, though some remain dialysis-dependent and overall mortality stays significant.
pitfalls: Withholding or stopping angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition because creatinine rises initially
Missing a normotensive presentation and attributing renal failure to another cause
Confusing the microangiopathy with primary thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and giving inappropriate plasma exchange alone
Using unnecessary glucocorticoids in high-risk early diffuse disease
references: EULAR recommendations for the treatment of systemic sclerosis
